content: Thalassaemia is an autosomal recessive blood disorder caused by mutations in the globin genes or their regulatory regions. These mutations result in a decreased production of one of the globin chains that form haemoglobin. In β-thalassaemia, there is a reduced synthesis of β-globin chains, which leads to an excess of free α-globin chains. The surplus α-globin chains precipitate within red blood cells, causing their increased destruction (haemolysis) and impairing the production of new red blood cells (ineffective erythropoiesis). The standard treatment for β-thalassaemia involves correcting haemoglobin levels through regular red blood cell transfusions. However, these transfusions lead to iron overload, which must be managed with iron chelation therapy. While early diagnosis and initiation of these supportive treatments have significantly improved the quality of life for individuals with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, the only widely available curative therapy is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Recently, gene therapy for β-thalassaemia has received conditional marketing approval in Europe and may soon become another curative option for individuals with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of various types of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in individuals with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, electronic databases, relevant journals, conference abstracts, and online trial registries. The most recent search was performed on April 7, 2021. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomised controlled trials comparing different types of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or comparing transplantation with standard therapy (regular transfusions and iron chelation). Two independent reviewers planned to extract data, assess the risk of bias using standard Cochrane methodologies, and evaluate the quality of evidence using the GRADE approach. However, no trials meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. The main finding of this review is that no relevant randomised controlled trials or quasi-randomised controlled trials were retrieved after an extensive search of the literature. Consequently, there is no high-level evidence available to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of different types of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in individuals with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia. The authors concluded that the lack of robust evidence highlights the urgent need for well-designed, adequately powered randomised controlled trials to assess the effectiveness and safety of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in this population.
